correctness.rationale: Exact principal-minor checks on the 43 connected labeled graphs at orders 2–4 give I+A/2 positive semidefinite, making I+beta*A positive definite for 0<beta<1/2. The strictly concave potential has a unique orthant maximizer, the Nash equilibrium; for interior x it satisfies (I+beta*A)x=1 and the sum of player payoffs is ||x||²/2. Adding edge ij subtracts beta*x_i*x_j from the potential, so at the new interior optimizer its value is strictly smaller than the old maximum. The optimum equals T/2, proving strict fall of total action for every admissible transition. Independent mask enumeration and exact symbolic differences recovered one three-vertex and six four-vertex transition classes; the star and paw impose respective upper interior endpoints 1/3 and sqrt(2)-1. All payoff differences and the Bernstein sign certificates agree with the bound proof. The strictly decreasing C and Q start positive and become negative at their stated upper endpoints; the exact rational brackets locate the unique sign change in each. At alpha and gamma the corresponding payoff differences are zero, not negative; among the other transition classes all admissible comparisons strictly decrease payoff. At beta=3/8 the cycle-to-diamond witness gives Delta T=-12/91 and Delta W=276/8281. To replay, enumerate the connected masks and single missing edges modulo simultaneous vertex permutations, then compute the differences of the squared norms of the two symbolic solutions divided by two and check the signs as in RESULT.md lines 23–88. No uploaded verifier was run. These checks concern common-beta, interior comparisons, not corner equilibria.

value.rationale: It is natural to ask whether reduced play from more competition also reduces the sum of equilibrium payoffs. The exact four-player reversals show why the answer is no in the standard quadratic model, separating two economically meaningful observables. The minimality and complete threshold classification show where this is possible and exclude the other transition types, rather than reporting a single floating-point counterexample. The value does not rely on interpreting the payoff increase as large or on extrapolation to heterogeneous, larger, or corner-equilibrium games.
